q: What do like poles do?
a: They repel.

q: What do unlike poles do?
a: They attract.

q: Name four magnetic materials.
a: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.

q: What is a magnetically HARD material?
a: One that keeps its magnetism (hard to magnetise or demagnetise).

q: What is a magnetically SOFT material?
a: One that is easy to magnetise and loses its magnetism easily.

q: Give one use of a hard and one of a soft material.
a: Hard: permanent magnets. Soft: electromagnet cores.

q: What do magnetic field lines show?
a: The strength, direction and shape of the field.

q: Which way do field lines point outside a magnet?
a: From N to S.

q: Where is a bar magnet’s field strongest?
a: At the poles, where the lines are closest together.

q: What is induced magnetism?
a: A magnetic material becoming a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field.

q: What does a plotting compass show that iron filings do not?
a: The direction of the field.

q: What is a neutral point?
a: A point where two magnetic fields cancel, so the field is zero.

q: What is a uniform magnetic field?
a: One with the same strength and direction everywhere: parallel, equally spaced lines.

q: How do you make a uniform field?
a: Put a N pole facing a S pole, close together.

q: What is produced around a wire carrying a current?
a: A magnetic field.

q: What is the field shape around a straight wire?
a: Circles around the wire, closer together near the wire.

q: Why does a copper wire produce a magnetic field?
a: There is a current in the wire.

q: What is the field inside a solenoid like?
a: Strong and uniform: parallel lines.

q: What does the field outside a solenoid look like?
a: Like the field of a bar magnet.

q: Describe the construction of an electromagnet.
a: A coil of insulated wire wound on a soft iron core.

q: Name three ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
a: More current, more turns on the coil, an iron core.

q: Why is the core of an electromagnet soft iron?
a: It loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.

q: When is there no force on a charge moving in a magnetic field?
a: When it moves parallel to the field.

q: In which direction is the force on a moving charge?
a: At right angles to the field and to the motion.

q: Why does a force act on a current-carrying wire in a field?
a: The wire’s own field interacts with the magnet’s field.

q: Which hand is used in Fleming’s rule for motors?
a: The left hand.

q: In the left-hand rule, the first finger shows…
a: The field (N to S).

q: In the left-hand rule, the second finger shows…
a: The current (+ to −).

q: In the left-hand rule, the thumb shows…
a: The motion (the force).

q: How do you reverse the force on a wire?
a: Reverse the current OR the field (not both).

q: How do you increase the force on a wire?
a: A larger current or a stronger magnet.

q: What is the force on a wire lying parallel to the field?
a: Zero.

q: What does the split-ring commutator do?
a: Reverses the current every half turn so the coil keeps turning the same way.

q: Why does the coil of a d.c. motor turn?
a: The current is opposite on the two sides, so the forces are opposite.

q: How does a loudspeaker work?
a: a.c. in a coil in a magnet’s field makes the force keep reversing, so the cone vibrates and makes sound.

q: When is a voltage induced in a coil?
a: When there is relative movement between coil and magnet (field lines are cut).

q: What voltage is induced by a magnet held still in a coil?
a: Zero.

q: Name three ways to increase an induced voltage.
a: Move faster, stronger magnet, more turns on the coil.

q: Why is the output of a generator alternating?
a: The coil cuts the field in opposite directions each half turn.

q: What do slip rings do?
a: Keep the rotating coil connected to the external circuit.

q: Motor or generator: electrical energy to movement?
a: Motor. (A generator turns movement into electrical energy.)

q: Name the three parts of a transformer.
a: Primary coil, secondary coil and soft iron core.

q: How does a transformer work?
a: a.c. in the primary makes a changing field; this induces a voltage in the secondary.

q: Why does a transformer need a.c.?
a: d.c. gives a steady field, so no voltage is induced.

q: Step-up or step-down: more turns on the secondary?
a: Step-up. (Step-down has fewer.)

q: Write the turns-ratio equation.
a: Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns

q: Write the power equation for a transformer.
a: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is (100% efficient)

q: Why is electricity transmitted at high voltage?
a: Lower current, less heating of cables, less energy wasted.

q: Why use step-down transformers near homes?
a: To give a safe voltage (230 V).

q: What assumption is made in VpIp = VsIs?
a: The transformer is 100% efficient: no energy is lost.

q: Vp = 6.0 V, Np = 100, Ns = 400. Find Vs.
Vp = 230 V, Vs = 12 V, Np = 1150. Find Ns.
a: 60 turns

q: State the units of current, voltage and power.
a: Ampere (A), volt (V), watt (W).
